list.listitem: Bacterial rhinosinusitis is more likely in patients with preceding cold, unilateral tender maxillary sinuses, maxillary toothache, and purulent nasal discharge. It is also more likely in patients with more severe symptoms, and possibly in those who initially improve and then worse with an upper respiratory infection. B
Imaging is not routinely recommended. C

For patients with mild-to-moderate symptoms, provide symptomatic relief and reassurance; prescribe antibiotics for those with severe symptoms or impaired immune competence. Given the limited benefit, high prevalence of adverse events, antibiotic resistance, and the very low incidence of serious complications, antibiotics should be prescribed only when there is clear suspicion of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis or when symptoms are severe or prolonged. B

background.definition: Acute sinusitis is an inflammation of one or more of the paranasal sinuses that resolves in less than 12 weeks. Because rhinitis and sinusitis usually coexist, "rhinosinusitis" has become the preferred term. The sinuses most commonly affected are the maxillary and ethmoidal sinuses. Isolated inflammation of the frontal or sphenoidal sinuses is rare.

list.listitem: Adults have two to three viral upper respiratory tract infections (URIs) per year; most of these colds are accompanied by viral rhinosinusitis.
Studies that have performed culture of antral puncture fluid in adults with clinically suspected rhinosinusitis have detected pathogenic bacteria in about one-third of patients.
While acute bacterial rhinosinusitis is diagnosed in 16% of the US adult population annually, this is likely an overestimate since it is based on clinical diagnosis.
Allergic fungal sinusitis is the cause of between 6% and 9% of rhinosinusitis cases requiring surgery.
In one study of 112 children with URIs, 8% developed sinusitis; 60% of children with sinusitis have a bacterial cause (CDC).
Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis imposes an overall direct annual healthcare cost in the United States of $5.8 billion.
Acute rhinosinusitis is one of the 10 most common diagnoses in ambulatory practice.

It is the fifth most common diagnosis for which antibiotics are prescribed and is the cause of an estimated 3.3 million primary care office visits in 2008 (CDC). Sinusitis accounts for 15% to 21% of adult outpatient antibiotic prescriptions.

Authors of a systematic review and metaanalysis found that infectious sinusitis affected 27% of mechanically-ventilated patients, was the cause of undetermined fever in 25% of the cases, and is a risk factor for pneumonia.
Viruses: rhinovirus, coronavirus, influenza A and B, parainfluenza, respiratory syncytial virus, adenovirus, enterovirus.
Bacteria (about 30% of patients with clinically diagnosed acute rhinosinusitis): Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis.
Other (less common): allergens, local irritants.
Fungal: Aspergillus sp. In one cases series of 76 patients in India, Aspergillus flavus (75%) was most common followed by Aspergillus niger (10%), Schizophyllum commune (10%) and Alternaria (5%).

Acute bacterial rhinosinusitis is only rarely a complication of an acute sore throat; only 1% of adults with acute sore throat develop a suppurative complication such as peritonsillar abscess, otitis media, skin infection or sinusitis.
Acute rhinosinusitis typically starts with a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract that involves both the nasal passages and the paranasal sinuses.
Nasal fluid containing viruses, bacteria, and inflammatory mediators accumulates in the sinuses, where they produce inflammation, infection, or both.
This results in mucosal edema, cellular infiltration, and mucus thickening in the sinuses.
In a minority of cases, secondary bacterial infection occurs.

The causes of secondary bacterial infection are largely unknown, but obstruction of the sinus ostia, nose blowing, local/systemic immunity, the virulence of the virus, colonization of the nasopharynx with potential bacterial pathogens, and various environmental factors may play a role.

Fungal rhinosinusitis is divided into non-invasive (allergic fungal rhinosinusitis and fungus ball) and invasive (acute or chronic invasive fungal rhinosinusitis and chronic invasive granulomatous fungal rhinosinusitis). Based on a case series of 400 patients, the vast majority (87.25%) were non-invasive. Indoor air exposure to fungi, genetic predisposition and structural factors likely play a role. In addition, fungi can be directly allergenic when colonizing the respiratory tract or indirectly through contact with cell wall constituents and proteases, causing or exacerbating allergic disease.
Most cases of rhinosinusitis are caused by viruses. B
The clinical picture of bacterial and viral rhinosinusitis is very similar. B

Bacterial rhinosinusitis is more likely in patients with preceding cold, unilateral tender maxillary sinuses, maxillary toothache, and purulent nasal discharge. It is also more likely in patients with more severe symptoms, and possibly in those who initially improve and then worsen (ie, double sickening). B

Other than sinus puncture and culture, no diagnostic tests accurately discriminate patients with viral rhinosinusitis from patients with bacterial rhinosinusitis. Imaging is, therefore, not routinely recommended. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Sneezing, watery rhinorrhea, nasal itching, itchy watery eyes
Attacks of headache, unilateral pain, absence of nasal symptoms
Chronic complaints of unilateral discharge or obstruction
Pain made worse by hot and cold drinks or by chewing
Duration greater than 12 weeks for chronic sinusitis
Toxic appearance, headache, ocular manifestations (CN VI palsy) in patient with sinusitis or other facial infection.

list.listitem: European Position Paper on Rhinosinusitis and Nasal Polyps (2007): sudden onset of two or more symptoms, one of which should be either nasal blockage/obstruction/congestion or nasal discharge (anterior/posterior nasal drip) in combination with facial pain or pressure, or reduction/loss of smell. Acute nonviral rhinosinusitis is characterized by an increase in rhinosinusitis symptoms after 5 days or persistent symptoms after 10 days (with <12 weeks of duration).

The Infectious Disease Society of America (IDSA) recommends a diagnosis of acute sinusitis when symptoms or signs of acute rhinosinusitis (purulent nasal drainage accompanied by nasal obstruction, facial pain-pressure-fullness, or both) persist without evidence of improvement for at least 10 days beyond the onset of upper respiratory symptoms OR symptoms or signs of acute rhinosinusitis worsen within 10 days after an initial improvement.

Position paper endorsed by the CDC, the American Academy of Family Physicians, the American College of Physicians, the American Society of Internal Medicine, and the Infectious Diseases Society of American (2001): symptoms most helpful in predicting acute bacterial sinusitis are purulent nasal discharge, maxillary toothache or facial pain (especially unilateral), unilateral maxillary sinus tenderness, and worsening symptoms after initial improvement.
However, the diagnostic criteria are neither sensitive nor specific for distinguishing viral from bacterial infection.

Acute rhinosinusitis (viral or bacterial) typically presents with symptoms such as nasal blockage, congestion or stuffiness, nasal discharge or postnasal drip, facial pain or pressure, headache, or reduction/loss of smell.

In a case series of children (ages 3-12 years) in Taiwan, the most troublesome symptoms among the 69 subjects with acute rhinosinusitis were postnasal drip, nasal obstruction and cough. The most troublesome symptoms among the 27 children with acute rhinosinusitis combined with allergic rhinitis were nasal obstruction, postnasal drip, and itchy eyes.
In a systematic review including 807 patients with acute invasive fungal sinusitis, the most common presenting symptoms were facial swelling (64.5%), fever (62.9%), and nasal congestion (52.2%).
The general clinical impression is moderately accurate (LR+ 3.3, LR− 0.4).

Symptoms lasting for 10 days or longer or worsening symptoms (especially after initial improvement ["double sickening"]) increase the likelihood of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (ABRS). Other symptoms that increase the likelihood of ABRS somewhat include the presence of purulent nasal discharge, maxillary toothache, facial pain (especially unilateral), or unilateral maxillary sinus tenderness.

In the presence of severe or worsening symptoms with profuse nasal discharge, facial pain, and systemic symptoms, bacterial infection is more likely.In a study of 175 adults all undergoing CT and/or antral puncture, the best independent predictors of bacterial cause included preceding URI, absence of previous sinusitis diagnosis, unilateral tender maxillary sinusitis, maxillary toothache, purulent nasal discharge, and C-reactive protein (CRP) >15 mg/L.

The overall clinical impression ("clinical gestalt") is moderately accurate for diagnosis of acute rhinosinusitis in adults (LR+ 3.0, LR– 0.37) and a bit better for diagnosis of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in adults (LR+ 3.9, LR– 0.33).

Diagnostic tests are not routinely recommended, as there are no diagnostic tests that discriminate with sufficient accuracy between patients who have acute bacterial rhinosinusitis and patients who have viral rhinosinusitis.
An elevated CRP is a good predictor of acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, but is not available in all settings at the point of care.
There is evidence from 2 studies that use of procalcitonin may reduce antibiotic prescribing (42% in one study and 71% in another).

In one study of children with a clinical diagnosis of acute sinusitis, absence of pathogens on nasopharyngeal culture was not helpful in reliably identifying the subgroup of children with normal radiographs.

IDSA recommends computed tomography (CT) scan (preferred) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to investigate noninfectious causes or suppurative complications for patients who have worsening or no improvement after 3 to 5 days of antibiotics that have been broadened or changed in response to initial treatment failure. IDSA also recommends meatal cultures for pathogen-specific therapy.
MRI may be more sensitive for detecting early changes of acute invasive fungal sinusitis than CT.
Bacterial sinusitis is unlikely in the presence of normal sinus radiographs. Ultrasound is not significantly more accurate than plain radiographs.

Air-fluid levels or unilateral opacity of a maxillary sinus on CT scan or plain x-ray increases the probability of bacterial infection but is not diagnostic. Absence of fluid is good evidence against bacterial rhinosinusitis, though.

If imaging is deemed necessary due to suspected orbital or intracranial complications, the American College of Radiology (2017) recommends MRI maxillofacial and head without and with contrast or CT of the paranasal sinuses with contrast. If an obstructing mass or fungal sinusitis is suspected, MRI maxillofacial without and with contrast and/or CT of the paranasal sinuses without contrast are most appropriate.

To reduce radiation exposure from CT, authors of one study found the iterative reconstruction technique allowed for significant dose reduction of up to 60% for paranasal-sinus CT without impairing diagnostic image quality.
Several decision rules for diagnosing bacterial rhinosinusitis are described in the literature. However, none has been prospectively validated.

Ebell and Hansen used a dataset of 175 Danish adults presenting to primary care with suspected acute sinusitis. All received CT and those with any fluid received antral puncture. About one-third had a bacterial cause identified. Predictors of bacterial cause included preceding URI, absence of previous sinusitis diagnosis, unilateral tender maxillary sinusitis, maxillary toothache, purulent nasal discharge, and CRP > 15 mg/L. A risk score was developed and internally validated.

The decision rule of Berg is based on a diagnostic trial of patients from an emergency department with symptoms of less than 3 months. The relevance of this study is limited by inclusion of patients whose symptoms lasted for more than 30 days. This rule has not been validated in another population.

The decision rule of Williams is based on a study of men with suspected rhinosinusitis in a Veterans Administration outpatient clinic. The reliability of this study is limited by the use of plain radiography as the reference standard. This study overestimates the presence of bacterial infection by as much as 50%, offering a large opportunity for misclassification. Likewise, this rule has not been validated in another population.

An individual patient data analysis of 3 studies created a model with the following predictors: previous diagnosis of ARS, preceding upper respiratory tract infection, anosmia, double sickening, purulent nasal discharge on examination, need for antibiotics as judged by a physician, and CRP. The AUC was 0.72.
In patients with symptoms lasting less than 10 days that are not worsening, assume acute viral rhinosinusitis and do not use antibiotics.
Consider antibiotics if worsening or severe symptoms are present or the patient has immune compromise.
Routine imaging studies are not required.
See for a suggested approach to acute rhinosinusitis.
Most cases of acute rhinosinusitis resolve without antibiotics. A
Treatment of pain is important. C For relief of nasal symptoms, consider decongestants or intranasal corticosteroids; the latter have evidence to support their benefit from a Cochrane review. B

There is mixed evidence about the effectiveness of antibiotics in patients with mild or moderate symptoms even when those symptoms last for more than 7 to 10 days. Cochrane authors concluded that given the limited benefit, high prevalence of adverse events, antibiotic resistance, and the very low incidence of serious complications, antibiotics should not be prescribed for adult patients with clinically diagnosed, uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis. B

The American College of Physicians and CDC recommend antibiotics for patients with persistent symptoms >10 days, onset of severe symptoms or signs of high fever (>39°C) and purulent nasal discharge or facial pain lasting for at least 3 consecutive days, or onset of worsening symptoms following a typical viral illness lasting 5 days that was initially improving. B
Patients in whom the suspicion of developing a complication exists should be referred immediately for diagnostic investigation and IV antibiotics. C

In an individual patient-level data meta-analysis including 9 RCTs with 2547 patients with clinical suspicion of acute rhinosinusitis, the NNT for antibiotics was 15 and the NNT to harm was 190. Contrary to common belief, older patients, those reporting symptom of longer duration, and those reporting more severe symptoms are no more likely to benefit from antibiotics.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 15 trials with 3057 patients, however, concluded that given similar benefits (46% cured after one week and 64% after 14 days without antibiotics), higher prevalence of adverse events (27% of those who received antibiotics vs. 15% of those who received placebo), antibiotic resistance, and the very low incidence of serious complications, antibiotics should not be prescribed for adult patients with clinically diagnosed, uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis. They estimate at best 5 to 11 more people cured faster out of 100 given antibiotics.

Authors of a meta-analysis concluded that newer and broad-spectrum antibiotics are not significantly more effective than narrow-spectrum agents; one meta-analysis found that risk of treatment failure was 3.5% lower with amoxicillin-clavulanate compared with cephalosporins at 10 to 25 days after treatment initiation.

The American College of Physicians and CDC recommend antibiotics for patients with persistent symptoms >10 days, onset of severe symptoms or signs of high fever (>39°C) and purulent nasal discharge or facial pain lasting for at least 3 consecutive days, or onset of worsening symptoms following a typical viral illness lasting 5 days that was initially improving.

IDSA guidelines recommend use of amoxicillin-clavulanate rather than amoxicillin alone for both adults C and children B. In addition, high dose (2 g orally twice daily or 90 mg/kg/day orally twice daily) amoxicillin-clavulanate is recommended for adults and children, respectively, from geographic regions with high endemic rates (>10%) of invasive penicillin-nonsusceptible S. pneumoniae, those with severe infection (eg, systemic toxicity with fever of 39ºC or higher and threat of suppurative complications), daycare attendance, age <2 years or >65 years, recent hospitalization, antibiotic use within the past month, or who are immunocompromised.

IDSA recommends a respiratory quinolone as a second-line agent; doxycycline can be used as an alternate agent in adults and combination therapy with a third-generation oral cephalosporin (cefixime or cefpodoxime) plus clindamycin may be used as second-line therapy for children with non-type I penicillin allergy or from geographic regions with high endemic rates of penicillin nonsusceptible S. pneumoniae.

IDSA recommends antibiotic duration of 5 to 7 days in adults and 10 to 14 days in children. An umbrella overview (a systematic review of systematic reviews) found no evidence that short course was inferior to long course antibiotics for acute sinusitis (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.81 - 1.21).

However, the IDSA guidelines are based largely on disease oriented evidence and expert opinion. A randomized trial with 157 participants compared amoxicillin 875 mg with clavulanate 125 mg plus either placebo or amoxicillin 875 mg twice daily for 7 days. There was no difference in outcomes.
There are no data from RCTs about whether antibiotic therapy is effective for sporadic or recurrent episodes of acute rhinosinusitis.

A systematic review identified two randomized trials evaluating the impact of procalcitonin (PCT) guided antibiotic therapy. Both studies demonstrated a significant reduction in antibiotic use with PCT guidance and no impact on duration of symptoms.

Individual studies of inhaled or oral steroids have not shown benefit in patients with acute sinusitis. Authors of a Cochrane systematic review found that patients taking intranasal corticosteroids had slightly greater resolution or improvement of symptoms compared to placebo (73% vs. 66%; NNT = 14), with higher dose steroids having a stronger effect. A meta-analysis confirmed small differences in resolution or improvement of symptoms with intranasal steroids. IDSA guidelines recommend intranasal steroids, especially in patients with a history of allergic rhinitis.

Intranasal corticosteroids are likely of benefit for adult patients with recurrent acute rhinosinusitis. Based on three trials, the difference for the median number of days to clinical success favored intranasal corticosteroids over placebo (6 days vs. 9 days, respectively).

Authors of a Cochrane review found that oral corticosteroids as monotherapy were ineffective for adult patients with acute sinusitis but appear to be of modest benefit in combination with antibiotics for short-term symptom relief.

Despite a lack of evidence, use of intramuscular or oral steroids is common for acute respiratory infections including sinusitis. Their use medicalizes the visit, leading to an increase in the likelihood of a second visit.
Decongestants (norephedrine, oxymetazoline, pseudoephedrine) provide short-term relief (3-10 hours) of congestive symptoms. IDSA does not recommend these for acute bacterial sinusitis.

Antihistamines and ipratropium bromide may improve runny nose and sneezing in viral rhinosinusitis or common cold. Authors of a meta-analysis of two RCTs found that loratadine decreased nasal obstruction in patients with allergic rhinitis accompanied by acute rhinosinusitis but had no benefit on total symptom score or rhinorrhea symptoms. IDSA does not recommend these for acute bacterial sinusitis.
For children with acute rhinosinusitis, a Cochrane review concluded that there is no evidence to determine whether antihistamines or decongestants are efficacious.
Mucolytics: In one small trial, the addition of oral acetylcysteine to amoxicillin-clavulanic acid, pseudoephedrine, and intranasal normal saline had no benefit in subacute sinusitis.

Nasal irrigation: Authors of a Cochrane review of nasal irrigation for adult patients with acute URI or rhinosinusitis found no clear benefit; trials were small and at high risk for bias. A later systematic review concluded that nasal irrigation was of limited efficacy for adult patients with acute rhinosinusitis. IDSA guidelines recommend intranasal saline as an adjunct in adults. It is of uncertain efficacy in children. A systematic review of 4 RCTs in 569 children 3 months to 12 years concluded that saline nasal irrigation could improve nasal but not respiratory symptoms, and might reduce antibiotic prescriptions.

Pain medication: There are no RCTs investigating the effectiveness of pain medication in rhinosinusitis. For symptomatic pain relief, acetaminophen is the first choice (2-4 g/d) because it is safe and well tolerated. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen (400 mg 3 times daily) or naproxen (200-500 mg twice daily) can also be used.

Inflammatory modulator: Nebulized high molecular weight sodium hyaluronate (3%) in saline solution in addition to levofloxacin and systemic steroids was helpful in reducing nasal discharge vs. placebo in one small RCT of patients with CT-confirmed acute rhinosinusitis.

In one case series, in-office balloon dilation of maxillary sinus ostia and ethmoid infundibula reduced mean numbers of acute sinus infections, antibiotic courses, and sinus-related physician visits in patients with either recurrent acute rhinosinusitis or chronic sinusitis at one-year follow-up.
The effectiveness of zinc, echinacea, steam inhalation, and saline spray is unknown for acute sinusitis.
Vitamin C is probably not effective.
In a RCT of a dry extract of 5 herbs (BNO 1016) vs. placebo, active treatment provided symptom relief two days earlier than placebo and was well tolerated.

A small trial randomized 100 patients with acute bacterial rhinosinusitis (confirmed by middle meatus aspirate) to EPs 7630 (pelargonium sidoides extract) 20 mg three times daily or amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily, each for 10 days. EPs 7630 resulted in greater improvement on a number of symptoms, but the differences were small and probably not clinically significant.
Refer or hospitalize the patient when symptoms or signs of a possible complication occur such as facial swelling; visual, orbital, meningeal, or cerebral symptoms; or symptoms of septicemia.
Consider referral in case of treatment failure after an extended course of antibiotics or frequent recurrences of acute rhinosinusitis, or if complaints last for more than 12 weeks.

IDSA recommends referral to a specialist for patients who are seriously ill and immunocompromised, continue to deteriorate clinically despite extended courses of antimicrobial therapy, or have recurrent bouts of acute rhinosinusitis.

Complications may arise from direct extension of the infection or hematogenous spread of infection and include: periorbital infection, orbital cellulitis, cavernous sinus thrombosis, pansinusitis, epidural abscess, subdural empyema, cerebral abscess, meningitis, osteomyelitis of the frontal bone, and septicemia.
When a complication is suspected, the patient should be immediately referred for diagnostic investigation and IV antibiotic therapy.
Without antibiotics, 46% of patients are free of symptoms after 7 days and 64% after 14 days. B
Ninety percent of patients are symptom free after 4 weeks. C
Complications are rare but can be serious; they occur in about 1 in 10,000 episodes. C
Among patients with acute invasive fungal rhinosinusitis, the overall survival rate is about 50%, despite use of intravenous antifungal medication and surgery. B
There is no evidence that chronic rhinosinusitis is a consequence of acute rhinosinusitis. C
